content: Uncontrolled bleeding is a significant cause of death in individuals who experience traumatic injuries. Antifibrinolytic drugs, which are known to reduce blood loss during surgical procedures, may also be effective in minimizing blood loss following trauma. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of antifibrinolytic drugs in patients with acute traumatic injuries. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted in January 2015. This included databases such as the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, The Cochrane Library, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and clinical trial registries. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials that investigated the use of antifibrinolytic agents, such as aprotinin, tranexamic acid (TXA), epsilon-aminocaproic acid, and aminomethylbenzoic acid, in patients with acute traumatic injuries. Two authors independently selected studies that met the inclusion criteria and extracted data. One author assessed the risk of bias in key domains. The outcomes measured included all-cause mortality at the end of follow-up, adverse events (such as vascular occlusive events like myocardial infarction, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism, as well as renal failure), the number of patients requiring surgical intervention or blood transfusion, the volume of blood transfused, the volume of intracranial bleeding, the presence of brain ischemic lesions, and death or disability. The quality of evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low using the GRADE approach. Three trials met the inclusion criteria. Two of these trials (n = 20,451) evaluated the effects of TXA. The larger trial, CRASH-2 (n = 20,211), was conducted across 40 countries and included patients with various types of trauma. The smaller trial (n = 240) focused exclusively on patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). The third trial (n = 77) assessed the use of aprotinin in patients with major bony trauma and shock. The pooled data demonstrated that antifibrinolytic drugs reduce the risk of death from any cause by 10% (relative risk [RR] 0.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85 to 0.96; P = 0.002). The quality of this evidence was rated as high. This finding was primarily based on data from the CRASH-2 trial, which contributed 99% of the data. There was no evidence to suggest that antifibrinolytic drugs increase the risk of vascular occlusive events (moderate-quality evidence) or affect the need for surgical intervention or blood transfusion (high-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the effects of different antifibrinolytic drugs (e.g., TXA versus aprotinin). However, since the pooled analyses were predominantly based on data from trials involving TXA, the results are most applicable to TXA. The effects of aprotinin in this patient population remain uncertain. In patients with TBI, there is some evidence suggesting that TXA may reduce mortality, but the estimates are imprecise, the quality of evidence is low, and uncertainty persists. There is stronger evidence indicating that TXA may reduce intracranial bleeding in this population. The authors concluded that TXA safely reduces mortality in trauma patients with bleeding and does not increase the risk of adverse events. TXA should be administered as early as possible and within three hours of injury, as further analysis of the CRASH-2 trial indicated that treatment beyond this time frame is unlikely to be effective and may even be harmful. While there is some promising evidence regarding the use of TXA in patients with TBI, significant uncertainty remains. Two ongoing trials focusing on patients with isolated TBI are expected to address these uncertainties.
